questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a listener hears the end of a movement
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a cadence signals the close of a movement.
questions.stem: Editor's query 21 asks the team to explain how a listener usually recognises the end of a movement.

answer.exemplar: The clearest signal of the close is a strong cadence, most often a perfect authentic cadence in which the dominant moves to the tonic and the melody lands on the tonic note, so the key is confirmed rather than merely suggested. Around that moment composers pile on further cues: the texture thins out, the tempo slows, the bass drops to its lowest register, and the final chord is held longer than the notes around it. A listener reads all of these together, not one alone, as the movement coming to rest.

questions.explanation: A strong cadence, usually a dominant resolving to the tonic, confirms the key and tells the listener the music has settled. A longer final note, a slower tempo and a thinner texture reinforce that message.
questions.hint: Think of the chord that finally confirms the key.

options.misconception: Confuses the note count with the converted duration.

options.text: It prints 3, because six eighth notes are worth three quarter notes.
It prints 2, because the code divides by the number of beats in the bar.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A fugue's answer against its subject
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the intervals of a fugal answer are adjusted.
questions.stem: Translator's footnote 30 asks the team to explain why the intervals of a fugal answer are adjusted when the subject moves to the dominant.

answer.exemplar: In a tonal fugue the answer is the subject moved to the dominant, but the transposition cannot be exact. Certain notes of the subject would land badly in the new key, most obviously the leading note, and the composer adjusts them, turning a third into a second or a sixth into a fifth so that the line still fits the harmony. The result is an answer that is recognisably the same tune but made to live in its new key, which is what distinguishes a tonal answer from a strict real answer at the fifth.

questions.explanation: A literal transposition would clash with the new key, so a tonal answer alters a note or two to make the harmony work. The melody still reads as the subject, which keeps the reply intelligible.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the harmony.

questions.topic: The total duration of a 12/8 measure
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a 12/8 bar is felt in four beats.
questions.stem: Translator's note 16 asks the team to explain why a 12/8 bar is felt in four beats rather than twelve.

answer.exemplar: A bar of 12/8 is written with twelve eighth notes, but the pulse of the music comes from the way those notes are grouped. The twelve are heard in four groups of three, and each group of three eighths makes one dotted quarter note, so the bar is felt in four beats. The same twelve notes written as 12/4 would be a very different piece, because the bar would then hold twelve quarter notes.

questions.explanation: The twelve eighth notes are grouped in threes, and each group of three is a dotted quarter note. That makes 12/8 compound quadruple, so the listener feels four beats while the notation shows twelve notes.
questions.hint: Group the twelve eighth notes in threes.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Modulation and the pivot chord
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a pivot chord carries a modulation between two keys.
questions.stem: Translation note 51 asks the team to explain how a single chord can carry a modulation from one key into another.

answer.exemplar: A pivot chord is a chord that can be heard in two different keys at once, and composers use it to make a modulation sound like a natural continuation rather than a jump. The chord arrives in the old key, doing its usual job there, and then the following harmony reveals that it has been re-read in the new key, where it has a different name and a different function. A second-in-the-old-key chord that becomes the fourth in the new key is a common example, and the ear accepts the change because the chord itself never had to move.

questions.explanation: A pivot chord belongs to both keys, and the ear accepts it in the first key before it is reinterpreted in the second. That single moment of shared meaning is the point where the new key takes over.
questions.hint: The chord must be able to belong to both keys.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The sections of sonata form
questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of the development section.
questions.stem: Translator's note 88 asks the team to explain what the development section is for in a sonata form movement.

answer.exemplar: The development is where the music already established is turned loose. Its themes are usually fragmented, sequenced and moved into remote keys, sometimes with the material almost dissolved into a continuous passage, and this is what removes the listener's sense of which key the music is in. That uncertainty is the point of the section, because it makes the recapitulation, where the first theme returns in the tonic, sound like a homecoming rather than merely a repetition.

questions.explanation: The development works the exposition's themes in unfamiliar keys and sequences, dissolving the sense of home. That instability is what makes the return of the tonic in the recapitulation feel like an arrival.
questions.hint: Ask what the section does to the themes it inherits.

questions.topic: Theme and variations
questions.learningObjective: Explain what keeps a theme recognisable across a set of variations.
questions.stem: Translation note 77 asks the team to explain what lets the listener still recognise the theme after several variations.

answer.exemplar: The listener keeps hold of the theme because each variation preserves enough of its shape for the ear to recognise it. Usually the opening contour, the rhythm of the first phrase and the general character stay put, while one element is reworked: the harmony, the melody's ornamentation, the tempo, the register, the metre or the number of voices playing. The gradual drift is what gives a set its shape, because the listener can always relate each new version back to the tune they heard at the start.

questions.explanation: Each variation alters one or two aspects of the theme and leaves its outline and character recognisable. Change too much at once and the listener loses the thread, so good variations change steadily.
questions.hint: Think about how much is left unchanged each time.

questions.stem: Translator's note 170 asks the team to explain what the transition does in a sonata form exposition.

answer.exemplar: The transition is the connective tissue of the exposition. It has to carry the music from the primary theme in the tonic across to the secondary theme in the dominant, and it does that by running the harmony through a sequence that gradually increases the pull towards the new key. Because the modulation is prepared rather than announced, the arrival of the second theme sounds like the inevitable next stage rather than a change of scene, and the closing section that follows can then confirm the dominant with confidence.

questions.explanation: The transition links the primary theme in the tonic to the secondary theme in the dominant, usually with a sequence that moves the harmony towards the new key. Its close is where that key is first heard.
questions.hint: Ask what the passage has to do between two themes.

answer.exemplar: The silence that follows the final chord is not empty space but part of the ending. It gives the listener a moment in which to hear the cadence settle, so the final chord is understood as a conclusion rather than as a stop. An empty bar after the chord also confirms that nothing more is coming, which matters because a movement that simply ceases on a chord can easily sound interrupted rather than complete.

questions.stem: Preface note 21 asks how many beats a 6/8 measure is felt in when it is counted as compound duple.

options.text: Three beats, one for each pair of eighth notes in the bar.
options.misconception: Groups the six eighths in twos instead of threes.

options.text: Six beats, one for each of the six eighth notes in the bar.
options.misconception: Counts the written notes and ignores the grouping.

options.text: Two beats, each a dotted quarter note made of three eighths.
One beat, because the whole bar is a single dotted half note.
options.misconception: Treats the bar as one undivided pulse.

questions.explanation: Six eighth notes group into two sets of three, and each set of three eighths is a dotted quarter note. That makes 6/8 compound duple, two beats of a dotted quarter each.
questions.hint: Group the six eighth notes in threes.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The total duration of a 12/8 measure
questions.learningObjective: Compare compound bars from a table of values.
questions.stem: Editorial note 66 tabulates compound bars: 6/8 holds 6 eighth notes, 9/8 holds 9, 12/8 holds 12 and 15/8 holds 15. How much longer than a 6/8 bar is a 15/8 bar, in eighth notes?

options.text: Fifteen eighth notes, because the code reports the total and not the difference.
options.misconception: Reports the full length instead of the comparison.

options.text: Six eighth notes, because the difference is the smaller of the two top numbers.
options.misconception: Subtracts the top numbers of the wrong bars.

options.text: Three eighth notes, because only the extra beats count toward the length.
options.misconception: Counts beats added to a common pulse instead of notes.

options.text: Nine eighth notes, because 15 minus 6 gives 9.

questions.explanation: Fifteen eighth notes against six gives a difference of nine eighth notes, that is four and a half quarter notes. All four bars are compound, so their top numbers are directly comparable.
questions.hint: Subtract the shorter total from the longer one.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Theme and variations
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the theme supplies to the variations that follow it.
questions.stem: Glossary draft row 2 asks the team to explain what the theme gives to the variations that follow it.

answer.exemplar: The theme is the tune the set is built on and the only statement the listener is guaranteed to hear in full. Every later version is measured against it, so a listener who has heard the theme can tell at once whether a variation has preserved the tune, embellished it, or moved far away from it. Because the set depends on that comparison, composers usually state the theme alone and unhurried at the start, so that its shape is clear before the variations begin.

questions.explanation: The theme supplies the material and the point of comparison, so the listener can hear each version against the tune they first heard. Without that first statement there would be nothing to vary.
questions.hint: Think about what the listener compares later.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A fugue's answer against its subject
questions.learningObjective: Count how much of the subject has sounded when the answer begins.
questions.stem: Translator's note 190 describes a fugue whose subject runs to eight bars and whose answer enters two bars after the leader begins. How many bars of the subject have already sounded when the answer starts?
questions.explanation: The answer enters two bars after the leader starts, so two bars of the subject have already sounded. That overlap is what lets the two voices interlock as counterpoint rather than merely alternate.
questions.hint: Count the bars between the leader's start and the answer.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The sections of sonata form
questions.learningObjective: Order the parts of a sonata form exposition.
questions.stem: Translator's note 200 asks which option lists the parts of a sonata form exposition in the order they usually appear.

options.text: Secondary theme, primary theme, transition, then closing section.
options.misconception: Starts the exposition with the theme in the dominant.

options.text: Primary theme, transition, secondary theme, then closing section.
Primary theme, secondary theme, transition, then closing section.
options.misconception: Swaps the transition and the second theme.

options.text: Primary theme, transition, closing section, then secondary theme.
options.misconception: Moves the closing section ahead of the second theme.

questions.explanation: The exposition opens with the primary theme in the tonic, moves through a transition, reaches the secondary theme in the dominant and finishes with a closing section that settles the new key.
questions.hint: Start with the theme in the tonic and work forward.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a listener hears the end of a movement
questions.learningObjective: Trace a check for the cues that mark a movement's ending.
questions.stem: Translator's note 208 traces this helper: cues := ['slow tempo', 'tonic cadence', 'held chord']; if 'tonic cadence' in cues and 'held chord' in cues: print('clear ending'). What is printed?

options.text: It prints clear ending, because any list of cues qualifies as an ending.
options.misconception: Believes the test checks for the presence of any cue.

options.text: It prints nothing, because the test needs all three cues to be present.
options.misconception: Assumes the condition requires every cue in the list.

options.text: It prints clear ending, because the trace contains both the cadence and the held chord.
It prints clear ending, because the list is in the order a movement normally ends.
options.misconception: Reads the order of the list as the test itself.

questions.explanation: The trace lists both a cadence in the tonic and a held final chord, so the condition passes. The tempo is present as well, and all three cues together leave the listener in no doubt about the close.
questions.hint: Check which cues the condition actually requires.
